change: The tiltrotor now tilts. Its ducts sat pointing up whatever the aircraft was doing, so a transition looked like a multirotor accelerating. change: The network no longer flashes at the end of the opening flight. The hand-over made the held-back layers visible and then asked for a frame; that frame was drawn before any fade had touched them, at full strength, and only the next preRender found them and dropped them to nothing - a flash, a blink, then the slow appearance. Re-read while something is faded out, transparent is recorded as full strength and it never comes back. That was invisible on a first load (the graphics are built after the entry starts) and would have shown on a second arrival. The controllers now have restart(), which empties the clock and keeps the colours.

change: Two changes aimed at drawing more aircraft. A billboard tier now sits between the point and the model: a glTF model is its own draw call and only about two dozen are affordable, while a whole BillboardCollection is one draw call at any count, so an aircraft past the model budget lands on a painted glyph instead of falling off a cliff to a three-pixel dot. That cliff was not only ugly, it churned - an aircraft demoted on one scan asked for its model back on the next. The glyph is painted once per kind and turned by heading in screen space (an icon, not an attitude); only entities whose size is known are promoted, because distance alone would put a glyph on each of thousands of satellites - the smear the point tier exists to condense, drawn larger. A model still loading falls back to its glyph; a model that FAILED still falls back to the point, because that is what the warning promises the operator. Where no canvas can be made the tier simply does not exist. Separately, while a scheduled day is on the map the satellites are no longer computed, encoded or sent at all: sixteen thousand orbits propagated per tick is the most expensive thing in the process and it shares the interpreter with the day.

change: Three decision charts - the PSU's sequencing, the pilot's guidance, the deck's pad and stands - drawn as the decisions they are, with the numbers each branch turns on sitting beside it. The rules were constants spread through three files, which is right for code and useless for an operator: 'ninety seconds between landings' means nothing until you can see it is the gap the next approach is pushed back by and that the branch under it is where an aircraft is told to wait. The charts travel from the server with the values, because a drawing kept in the browser drifts from the decision kept in the engine and it is always the drawing that starts lying. Saved values persist to one file and reset deletes it rather than writing the defaults into it, so a default that changes later still reaches an operator who never overrode it; a value out of range is clamped rather than refused, because the intent is legible and one mistyped field should not lose the other fifteen. The pilot's guidance numbers were compiled into the native library - how hard to brake and how early to leave the wing decide whether an approach takes four minutes or seventeen, which is an operating choice - so they were lifted into a RoutePilotTuning and a second C ABI entry point, every default the constant it replaced. change: People boarding in a replayed day were walking in jerks, and there were two causes multiplying together. The first: the layer asks the server who is walking every 1.5 seconds and, in between, redrew them at the elapsed time the server last gave - the maths that places a walker is perfectly continuous in time, but the time being handed to it never moved. So everyone stood still for a refresh and then teleported, six seconds' worth at four times speed. The comment above the loop even said it repaints every frame because people walk between fetches; the repainting was there and the advancing of the clock was not. The second: the update sat behind the 200 ms gate that throttles surface work, so it ran five times a second. The predicted flight path was already on the every-frame side of that gate for exactly this reason. Now the day's clock is carried forward between answers at the speed the day is actually running, measured from consecutive answers rather than passed in, so a pause reads as zero and nobody moves, a change of speed corrects itself within one refresh, and a jump or a step backwards is somebody dragging the clock rather than time passing and sets no speed at all. The carry is capped at one and a half refreshes so a walker can never run past where the next answer will put them: someone who pauses for a moment still reads as a person, someone who jumps backwards reads as a broken screen.

change: A vertiport in the PSU's occupancy list opens that deck. The list is one line each because the PSU is watching eighteen of them, and one line stops being enough the moment one of them matters - the answer to why is on the deck: which stands are taken, which pad is booked when, and who is in the queue in what order. The states come from real occupancy: a stand somebody is standing on reads differently from one somebody is only coming to, because whoever is deciding where to put an arrival has to be able to tell them apart; a pad is busy for a booking that covers now and spoken for only when one is close; a charger is in use when the aircraft on its stand is charging rather than merely parked on it; and a taxiway is coloured only where a ground run actually crosses it, found through the deck's own topology. change: A switch that takes the pilot's own waiting out of the picture. Asking why an aircraft is still waiting is hard to answer because the engine ORs four sources into one flag - PSU permission, the pilot's traffic call, terminal reservations, stand egress - so whichever is true first stops the aircraft and the screen says only that it is waiting. Every pilot-side wait is reached through one of two instructions, yield or wait_clear: the traffic flag reads them directly, the separation bay is only created for a yield, and the approach permission tests for them too. Downgrading those two to monitor in traffic_awareness closes all four paths at once, so what is left standing is PSU's. The warning survives with its reason extended, so the manoeuvre that did not happen is still in the record rather than silently gone, and the branch that keeps an already-yielding aircraft yielding across ticks honours the switch as well - without that the one aircraft being watched stays parked forever after the switch is thrown. Avoidance stays a separate switch, because not stopping is not the same as not looking: with self-hold off the pilot still keeps its distance laterally and by speed. The default is on, since a diagnostic switch must not change the day by existing.
